basics.name: Aadharsh Pannirselvam
basics.summary: I notice technology, take it apart to understand it, and write up what's inside. Obsessive about feel and performance: I live on beta and canary builds, give feedback, and lately ship the fixes. By day I invest in that frontier at Archetype, and the writing is part of that job; the rest of the time I tinker and play.

projects.name: Learning With Errors
highlights: Interactive technical explainers written as conversations: inline demos you can poke, a pop quiz at the end of each one. FHE, MPC, TEEs, UTF-8: hard things taught the way you'd actually pick them up, by taking them apart.

Garage study: disassembled thumbnail encoding: AVIF vs JPEG vs jpegli at the byte level, bytes-per-pixel benchmarks from my own measurements, plus experiments in image optimization, minifiers, and dictionary-based content compressors.
Among the first 10 solvers of Paradigm's Kryptos-style CTF puzzles, cracked with a group ideating constantly, AI in the loop. The Vigenère explainer above came out of that rabbit hole.

projects.name: Open-source contributor
highlights: Fixed the WebMCP standard on EmDash (a WordPress replacement) so hosted content is legible to AI agents, tracing the agent-readable web down to the protocol.
Improved the JavaScript minifier on Bun and Oxc, taking apart how code gets smaller.
Found that workerd's zstd silently dropped its dictionary option, filed it, and wrote the fix, pricing it against production first: 21.9% off 13 pages at roughly 0.2 ms of CPU each.
More merged work in the same lanes: Compression Dictionary Transport in web-platform-tests and MDN, and image-codec PRs into jxl-rs (libjxl) and zenjpeg.
Built houseguest, my personal software factory: a Claude Code plugin that makes my OSS contributions repeatable so PRs land mergeable, still being tweaked as I contribute more.

Thinking hard about how OSS maintenance evolves as AI-generated issues and PRs get cheap: what happens to feedback loops, and whether canaries and nightlies become the review process. I run both constantly.

projects.name: Internal tooling
highlights: Surveyed agent frameworks, then built a firmwide Slack AI agent on DigitalOcean Kubernetes around an open-source, extensible base, folding in lessons from each framework and my own tools. Plus a 20-skill sidekick toolkit; people across the firm use both daily, and I maintain them from usage metrics, feedback, what people build, and security developments.

work.name: Archetype
highlights: Wrote the 3-part "Privacy 2.0" series on privacy-enhancing technologies (TEEs, MPC, FHE, obfuscation), long-form research at the AI/crypto intersection that shaped the fund's applied-cryptography thesis.

Treated diligence as deep technical education: dug into parallel execution for distributed systems, eval design, model architectures, and audio processing for voice models. I learn the machinery first, then the market.
Mapped the agent-readable web: evangelized agent payment rails, onchain agents, and app-chain design through hands-on work with open-source builders.

Host and curate dinners and events gathering top technical people across cryptography, formal verification, and privacy, and have spoken on panels and MC'ed events in the space, including an Oxford-style debate on onchain agents.

work.name: Galaxy
highlights: Diligence on Mysten's Series A: benchmarked Sui's Move-based state concurrency model against Solana's parallelism and consensus protocol, applying broad distributed systems principles, and wrote internal directives on separated fee markets, applying game-theoretic principles and data.
